messages.content: I want to go to McDonald's and buy a pizza.

function.name: uber_eat_order
function.description: Place an order for food delivery on Uber Eats by specifying the restaurant and the items with their respective quantities. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

restaurant.description: The name of the restaurant from which to order food.

items.description: A list of food item names selected for the order.

quantities.description: A list of quantities for each food item, corresponding by index to the items array.

message.reasoning: The user wants to place an order for food delivery on Uber Eats. They want to go to McDonald's and buy a pizza. The user says "I want to go to McDonald's and buy a pizza." We need to interpret that as a request to place an order. The user wants to order a pizza from McDonald's. We need to use the function uber_eat_order. The function signature: uber_eat_order takes an object with keys: restaurant: string, items: string[], quantities: number[]. So we need to call the function with restaurant: "McDonald's", items: ["pizza"], quantities: [1]. That is presumably the correct usage. There's no mention of quantity or multiple items. The user wants to buy a pizza. So we can interpret that as ordering one pizza. So we call the function with restaurant: "McDonald's", items: ["pizza"], quantities: [1]. Then we need to respond with the function call. The user didn't ask for anything else. So we just call the function.
